Accessibility beyond mobility: describe layout and obstacles for low-vision residents, read mail and labels aloud, flash lights for the doorbell and alarms for deaf residents, keep furniture in consistent positions, dementia-friendly routines (labels, door checks).

section: Emergency response (must-have). Detection and alerting are covered well, but active response is thin.
text: Respond: shut off the main water, a fixture valve, or gas; use a fire extinguisher; evacuate people and pets; call emergency services and relay the address and symptoms; unlock the door and guide responders; fetch the AED and first-aid kit; run a power-outage routine (flashlights, unplug sensitive electronics, protect the fridge and freezer); shelter during severe weather; know where the breaker panel and shutoffs are.
Answer the doorbell or intercom; screen visitors and decline solicitors; let in expected guests; supervise repair people; accept and sign for deliveries.

Away mode. Your departure routine covers daily exits. Add a vacation or house-sitting mode: arm the alarm, set lights on timers, bring in mail and packages, water plants, check for leaks and pests, run taps, check the freezer after an outage, care for pets, send status photos.
“Hide this somewhere the dog can’t reach it.” Requires reasoning about the pet’s reach, jumping ability, room access, and object safety.
“Fix this up.” The robot must determine what looks wrong before deciding what actions to take.
“Finish whatever I forgot to do.” It needs to inspect the environment and infer incomplete chores.
“Check the house before we leave.” It has to inspect locks, windows, appliances, pets, lights, faucets, garage doors, and other household-specific concerns.
“Get the house ready for the morning.” It might prepare coffee equipment, bags, clothes, lunch items, blinds, and room temperature.
“Find something to prop this up.” Requires discovering an object based on physical affordances.
“Open this without spilling it.” Manipulation must adapt to unknown contents and container geometry.
“Move this through that doorway.” Requires rotating and maneuvering bulky objects.
“Make sure nothing looks wrong.” General anomaly detection across an open world.
“Check whether anything changed since I left.” Requires storing and comparing previous environmental states.
“Set things up how I like them.” Requires user-specific configuration memory.
“Make my room how it was yesterday.” Requires state reconstruction.
“Baby-proof this room.” Requires predicting how a small child could interact with the environment.
“Keep the cat out while you clean this room.” Requires simultaneous task execution and dynamic agent management.
“Don’t let the dog escape when you open the door.” Requires planning around another autonomous agent.
“Open the door for the delivery person but keep the pets inside.” Multi-agent dynamic reasoning.
“Do it without waking anyone up.” Requires reasoning about doors, floors, lights, vacuum noise, dishes, etc.
“Don't let anyone into the garage but me.” Requires persistent facial/voice recognition and the ability to politely refuse commands from unauthorized humans.
“Let me know if anyone suspicious comes to the door.” Requires differentiating between a regular delivery driver, a neighbor, and someone acting erratically or trying door handles.
“Open the door for that man.” or “Give me the knife.” (from a child) Requires deciding who can command what, refusing without escalating, and alerting an adult.
“Figure out how this washer works.” Requires reading the panel and manual, then testing options safely.
“We’re on a call, be quiet.” Requires switching to a quiet mode and blocking noisy interruptions (doorbell, vacuum, notifications).
